learning_outcomes.title: Law of Sines and the ambiguous case
learning_outcomes.statement: Determine whether three given measures define 0, 1, or 2 triangles using the Law of Sines.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Use a/sin A = b/sin B. For SSA, sin B = b sin A/a. Test both B₁ = sin⁻¹(value) and B₂ = 180° − B₁, accepting only cases with A + B < 180°. Opposite sides and angles share letters.

questions.title: A • All acute-angle boundary cases
questions.stem: In each case A = 30° and b = 10. Side a is opposite A and b is opposite B.

parts.prompt: Calculate h = b sin A and state its geometric meaning.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: h=10sin30°=5. It is the perpendicular height from the end of side b to the ray carrying side c. Award 2.

parts.prompt: Determine the number of triangles for a = 4, 5, 7, 10, and 12. Explain each classification.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: a=4<h gives 0; a=5=h gives 1 right triangle; 5<a=7<10 gives 2; a=10=b gives 1; a=12>b gives 1. Award 1 per correct classification with its comparison.

parts.prompt: For a = 5, find B and C. Explain why the count is one.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: sinB=10sin30°/5=1, so B=90° and C=60°. The supplementary B equals the same 90°, so it creates no second distinct triangle. Award 3.

questions.title: B • Solve both triangles
questions.stem: Given A = 40°, a = 9, and b = 12. Use degree mode. Keep full calculator precision until your final answers.

parts.prompt: Find sin B and the two candidate values of B.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: sinB=12sin40°/9≈0.85705. B₁≈58.986° and B₂≈121.014°. Award 1 for ratio and 2 for candidates.

parts.prompt: Check both candidates with the angle sum. State the number of triangles.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 40+58.986<180 and 40+121.014<180, so two triangles exist. Award 2.

parts.prompt: For each valid triangle, find C to the nearest degree and c to the nearest tenth.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: C₁≈81.014°→81°, c₁=9sinC₁/sin40°≈13.8. C₂≈18.986°→19°, c₂≈4.6. Award 1 per requested result.

parts.prompt: Explain why using only the inverse-sine output can miss a triangle.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: An acute and its supplementary obtuse angle have the same sine. Award 1.

questions.title: C • Obtuse angles and false candidates
questions.stem: Use the Law of Sines and the angle-sum condition.

parts.prompt: Given A = 120°, a = 8, b = 10, test the data and state the number of triangles.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: sinB=10sin120°/8≈1.0825>1, so no triangle exists. Award 3.

parts.prompt: Given A = 120°, a = 10, b = 8, determine the number of triangles and solve it. Round angles to the nearest degree and sides to the nearest tenth.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: sinB=8sin120°/10≈0.69282. B₁≈43.854° is valid, while B₂≈136.146° gives A+B₂>180°. Thus one triangle. B≈44°, C≈16°, and c=10sin(16.146°)/sin120°≈3.2. Award 1 for ratio, 1 for rejecting second angle, 1 for count, 1 for angles, 1 for c.

parts.prompt: For an obtuse A, explain why a must be greater than b for a triangle to exist.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: The side opposite the obtuse angle must be the longest side, so a>b. Award 2.
